STEMMER (NEDEFRA). Vi vil gerne klatre op med jer. Vi vasker os og er grundigt rene, men vi er for evigt golde. BEGGE KOR. Vinden er stille, stjernen tager flugten, den tungsindige måne skjuler sig gerne; trolddomskoret sprutter ildgnister frem i tusindtal i sit hvirvlende fremstød.
STEMME (NEDEFRA). Vent! Vent!
STEMME (OVENFRA). Hvem kalder der, fra kløften i klippen?

STEMME (NEDEFRA). Tag mig med! Tag mig med! Jeg har allerede klatret i tre hundrede år og kan stadig ikke nå toppen. Jeg vil være med mine fæller. BEGGE KOR. Kosten bærer, stokken bærer, høtyven bærer, gedebukken bærer. Den, der ikke kan løfte sig i nat, er fortabt for evigt. HALV-HEKS (NEDENFOR). Jeg har traskeret af sted al denne tid — hvor langt foran er de andre allerede! Jeg har ingen hvile derhjemme og får heller ingen her. HEKSEKOR. Salven giver heksene mod; en klud er god til et sejl; ethvert trug bliver et godt skib; den, der ikke har fløjet i nat, vil aldrig flyve. BEGGE KOR. Og når vi runder toppen, fejer hen over jorden og dækker heden vidt og bredt med jeres hekseskare. [De slår sig ned.]

MEPHISTOPHELES. Der skubbes og trænges, raller og rasler! Der fløjter og snurrer, mylres og pludres! Der glimter, gnistrer, stinker, brænder! Et ægte hekseelement! Men hold dig tæt til mig, ellers bliver vi adskilt på et øjeblik. Hvor er du?
FAUST (I DET FJERNE). Her!

MEPHISTOPHELES. Hvad! Allerede båret væk, så langt? Jeg må bruge min myndighed som mester. Plads! Junker Voland kommer! Gør plads, søde pak, gør plads! Her, Doktor, tag fat i mig, og lad os nu, i ét spring, komme klar af mængden. Det er for tosset selv for min slags. Lige derhenne skinner noget med et besynderligt lys. Noget drager mig hen mod de buske. Kom! Vi smutter derind.
FAUST. Du modsigelsens ånd! Men gå du foran — du må føre mig. Det var dog klogt gjort, ikke sandt: vi baner os vej til Brocken på Valborgsnat, blot for at isolere os her af eget valg.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Se blot på disse mangefarvede flammer! En lystig klub har samlet sig der. Man er ikke alene i et lille selskab.
FAUST. Jeg ville langt hellere være oppe ovenover! Jeg kan allerede se flamme og hvirvlende røg. Derhenne strømmer mængden til den Onde. Mangen en gåde må sikkert blive løst deroppe.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Og mangen en gåde er også knyttet her. Lad den store verden buldre, som den vil! Her slår vi os ned i fred. Det er gammel skik: i den store verden gør mænd sig små verdener. Derhenne ser jeg unge hekse, nøgne og bare, og gamle, der klogeligt holder sig tildækket. Vær venlig, om så blot for min skyld! Lidt besvær, masser af sport. Jeg hører instrumenter klinge. Forbandet skramleri! Man må vænne sig til det. Kom så, kom så! Det kan ikke være anderledes; jeg går foran og præsenterer dig, og jeg sætter dig i ny forpligtelse. Hvad siger du, min ven? Dette er ingen lille plads. Se blot! du kan næppe se enden af den! Hundrede ild brænder i en række. Folk danser, taler, koger, drikker, elsker! Sig mig nu — hvor kunne du finde noget bedre?
FAUST. For at præsentere os her, mener du at fremstille dig selv som troldmand eller som djævel?

MEPHISTOPHELES. Det er sandt, jeg er vel vant til at gå inkognito; men på gallafester viser man sine ordensdekorationer. Jeg har intet hosebånd at udmærke mig med, men kløften fod holdes i høj ære her. Ser du sneglen der? Hun kommer krybende op, og med sine følehorn har hun allerede vejret noget om mig. Selv om jeg ville, kunne jeg ikke forklæde mig her. Men kom! Vi går fra bål til bål; jeg er mellemmanden, og du skal være bejleren. [TIL NOGLE, DER SIDDER OMKRING UDDØENDE GLØDER.] Gamle herrer, hvad laver I herude i kanten? Jeg ville rose jer mere, hvis jeg fandt jer pænt i midten, i tummelens og ungdommens midte. Alene er man da nok hjemme. GENERAL. Hvem kan sætte sin lid til nationer, hvor meget man end har gjort for dem? For med folket, som med kvinderne, har ungdommen altid overhånd. MINISTER. I dag er folk vidt af den rette vej — giv mig de gode gamle! For sandelig, da vi var alt, dét var den sande guldalder.
FAUST. Jeg må gøre mit bedste for at bevare fatningen! Dette er et marked om en hals!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Hele stimmelen kæmper opad. Du tror, du skubber, og selv bliver du skubbet. FAUST. Hvem er da hun?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Mærk dig hende vel! Det er Lilith.
FAUST. Hvem?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Adams første hustru. Pas på hendes lyse hår, på det smykke, hvori hun stråler frem for andre. Når hun fanger en ung mand med det, slipper hun ham ikke så let igen.
FAUST. Der sidder to sammen, den gamle med den unge. De har allerede danset løs en god stund!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Der er ingen hvile for det selskab i nat. En ny dans begynder; kom, vi slutter os til.

FAUST (DANSER MED DEN UNGE). Jeg havde engang en yndig drøm: i den så jeg et æbletræ; to smukke æbler glimtede på det; de fristede mig, og jeg klatrede op. DEN SMUKKE. Små æbler har du altid begæret, og det gjorde du allerede i paradiset. Det rører mig med glæde, at min egen have også bærer sådanne frugter.

MEPHISTOPHELES (MED DEN GAMLE). Jeg havde engang en vild drøm. DEN GAMLE. Jeg fremfører min bedste respekt for ridderen af den kløftede fod. PROCKTOPHANTASMIST. Forbandede pak! Hvor vover I? Blev det ikke for længst påvist for jer, at en ånd aldrig står på almindelige fødder? Og nu står I her og danser løs som vi dødelige! DEN SMUKKE. Hvorfor kommer han da til vor bal?

FAUST (DANSER). Ha! Han er absolut overalt. Han skal bedømme alt, hvad andre danser! Hvis han ikke kan tale om hvert skridt, er skridtet så godt som aldrig gjort. Han er mest forarget, når vi går fremad. Hvis I blot ville dreje rundt i en cirkel, som han gør i sin gamle mølle, ville han nok kalde det godt — især hvis I gik hen og rådførte jer med ham om det. PROCKTOPHANTASMIST. Er I her stadig! Nej, dette er uhørt! Forsvind dog! Vi har oplyst verden, ved I ikke! Denne djævleyngel ænser ingen regler. Vi er så vise — og dog spøger det i Tegel trods alt! Hvor længe har jeg ikke fejet løs på vrangforestillingen, og dog bliver det aldrig rent! Det er uhørt! DEN SMUKKE. Stop dog med at kede os her, i det mindste! PROCKTOPHANTASMIST. Jeg siger jer ånder lige i ansigtet, jeg vil ikke tåle åndens despoti; min egen ånd kan ikke udøve det. [Dansen fortsætter.] I nat, ser jeg, vil intet lykkes for mig; men jeg er altid rede til en rejse, og jeg håber endnu, før mit sidste skridt, at få bugt med djævle og digtere.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Han vil straks sætte sig ned i en pyt — det er hans måde at berolige sig på; og når igler har frådset på hans bagdel, er han kureret for ånder og for ånd. [TIL FAUST, der har forladt dansen.] Hvorfor forlader du den smukke pige, der sang så sødt for dig i dansen?
FAUST. Ah! Midt i sangen sprang en lille rød mus ud af hendes mund.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Der er intet bemærkelsesværdigt i det. Man må ikke være for kræsen om sådanne ting. Det er nok, at musen ikke var grå. Hvem bryder sig om sligt i en elskovs time?
FAUST. Så så jeg — MEPHISTOPHELES. Hvad, menneske?

FAUST. Mephisto, ser du, derhenne, en bleg, dejlig pige, der står ene og fjernt? Hun slæber sig langsomt fra stedet; hun synes at gå med lænkede fødder. Jeg må tilstå, hun synes mig at ligne min stakkels

MEPHISTOPHELES. Hav intet at gøre med det! Intet godt kan komme deraf for nogen. Det er en magisk skikkelse, livløs — et afgudsbillede. Det er ikke godt at møde sligt; en mands blod isnes ved dets frosne blik, og han er nær ved at blive forvandlet til sten. Du har sikkert hørt om Medusa.
FAUST. Sandelig, dette er øjne af en, der er død, øjne, som ingen kærlig hånd var der til at lukke. Det er den barm, Margarethe overgav til mig; det er det søde legeme, jeg nød.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Det er trolddom, du letforførte tåbe; for hun antager, for hver mand, skikkelsen af hans egen elskede.
FAUST. Hvilken lykke! Hvilken lidelse! Jeg kan ikke rive mig løs fra det blik. Hvor sælsomt, at en enkelt rød linje, ikke tykkere end ryggen af en kniv, skulle pryde denne yndige hals.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Rigtigt! Det ser jeg også. Hun kan også bære hovedet under armen, eftersom Perseus har hugget det af for hende. Men stadig denne forkærlighed for vrangforestillinger! Kom dog op ad bakken; her er alt så lystigt som i Prateren, og medmindre jeg er forhekset, ser jeg sandelig et teater. Hvad foregår her da?

SERVIBILIS. De begynder igen straks. Et nyt stykke, det sidste af syv — det er skik her at give så mange. En dilettant har skrevet det, og dilettanter spiller det. Undskyld mig, mine herrer, men jeg må af sted. Det er mit dilettant-embede at hæve tæppet.
MEPHISTOPHELES. At finde dig her på Blocksbjerget — det er netop, hvad jeg billiger, for dette er det rette sted for dig.

chapters.title: Walpurgis-Night's Dream
paragraphs: [OR, OBERON AND TITANIA'S GOLDEN WEDDING. INTERMEZZO.]
STAGE-MANAGER. Today we rest for once, we, the brave sons of Mieding. Old mountain and damp dale—that is the whole scenery!
HERALD. For the wedding feast to be a golden one, fifty years must have passed; but if the quarrel is over, I shall like the Golden Wedding all the better.
OBERON. Spirits, if you are with me, this is the time to show it! The king and the queen are united once again.
PUCK. When Puck comes whirling himself about, and his foot goes whisking in the dance, hundreds come after him to share the joy.
ARIEL. Ariel rouses the song in tones of heavenly purity; his music draws many ugly faces, but it also draws the fair ones.

OBERON. Married couples who would agree—let them take their lesson from us two. To make a pair love each other, it is only necessary to part them. If the husband is sulky and the wife is fretting, take hold of them both at once. Lead her south for me, and him to the far ends of the north. ORCHESTRA-TUTTI (FORTISSIMO). Snouts of flies and noses of gnats, with all their kin, frog in the leaves and cricket in the grass—they are the musicians.
SOLO. See, here comes the bagpipe! It is the soap-bubble. Listen to its schnick-schnack through its blunt nose.
SPIRIT THAT IS FASHIONING ITSELF. Spider's foot and toad's belly, and little wings for the little fellow! It doesn't quite add up to a tiny creature, true, but it makes a little poem.
A PAIR OF LOVERS. Small step and high bound, through honey-dew and exhalations. Truly, you trip lightly enough for me, but you don't rise into the air.

INQUISITIVE TRAVELLER. Isn't this masquerading mockery? Can I believe my eyes? To see Oberon, the beautiful god, here tonight too! ORTHODOX. No claws, no tail! And yet beyond a doubt, just like the gods of Greece, he too is a devil. What I'm catching now is only a rough sketch; but I'll prepare myself in good time for the Italian journey.
PURIST. Ah! My ill luck brings me here; what an endless scene of rioting! And out of the whole host of witches, only two are powdered.
YOUNG WITCH. Powder, like petticoats, is for old, grey little women. So I sit naked upon my he-goat and show off a strapping body.
MATRON. We have too much breeding to squabble with you here; but I do hope you will rot, young and delicate as you are.
LEADER OF THE BAND. Snouts of flies and noses of gnats, don't swarm so about the naked one. Frog in the leaves and cricket in the grass, do please keep time.
WEATHERCOCK (TOWARDS ONE SIDE). Company to one's heart's content! Truly, nothing but brides! And bachelors, one for one—the most promising people!
WEATHERCOCK (TOWARDS THE OTHER SIDE). And if the ground does not open and swallow them all up, I'll jump into hell myself, and at a run.
XENIEN. We are here as insects, with sharp little nippers, to honour Satan, our worshipful papa, as befits his dignity.
HENNINGS. See how naively they joke together in a crowded troop. In the end they'll claim they have good hearts.

MUSAGET. I'm only too glad to lose myself in this host of witches; for truly, I could lead them more easily than the Muses. CI-DEVANT GENIUS OF THE AGE. With the right sort of people, one becomes somebody. Come, take hold of my coat-tail! The Blocksberg, like the German Parnassus, has a very broad summit.

INQUISITIVE TRAVELLER. Tell me, what is the name of that stiff man? He stalks along with proud steps; he sniffs at everything he can sniff at. He is scenting out Jesuits. THE CRANE. I like to fish in clear waters and even in troubled ones. That's why you see the pious gentleman associating even with devils. WORLDLING. Yes, for the pious, believe me, everything becomes a vehicle. They actually form many a little conventicle here upon the Blocksberg. DANCER. Isn't a new chorus coming? I hear drums in the distance. But don't trouble yourselves! It's only the monotonous bitterns among the reeds. DANCING MASTER. How each throws his legs about, gets on as best he can! The crooked one jumps, the clumsy one hops, and never asks how it looks.
FIDDLER. How deeply this pack of ragamuffins hate each other, and how gladly they would deal each other the finishing blow! The bagpipe unites them here, as Orpheus' lyre united the beasts.
DOGMATIST. I will not let myself be led astray by the cries of criticism or by doubts. The devil, however, must be something; for otherwise how could there be devils?
IDEALIST. Phantasy, this once, is really too masterful in my mind. Truly, if I am all that I see, then I must be beside myself today.
REALIST. Existence is a regular plague to me and cannot but vex me much. For the first time, I'm not standing firm upon my feet.

SUPERNATURALIST. I am greatly pleased to be here, and delighted with these creatures; for from devils I can certainly draw conclusions about good spirits. SCEPTIC. They follow the track of the flame and believe themselves close to the treasure. Only doubt (Zweifel) rhymes with devil (Teufel). Here I am quite at home.

LEADER OF THE BAND. Frog in the leaves and cricket in the grass, you confounded dilettantes! Snouts of flies and noses of gnats, you are real musicians! THE ADROIT. Sansouci—that is the name of this band of merry creatures; there is no longer any walking on feet, and so we walk upon our heads. THE AWKWARD. In times past we have sponged many a tasty morsel; but now, goodbye to all that! Our shoes are worn through with dancing; we run on bare soles. WILL-O'-THE-WISPS. We come from the bog from which we have only just sprung; but here in the dance we'll be the glittering gallants in no time.
SHOOTING STAR. From on high, in starlight and firelight, I came shooting down; now I lie sprawled crookedly in the grass—who will help me back onto my legs?
THE MASSIVE ONES. Room! Room! And spread out around! Down go the blades of grass. Spirits are coming, but spirits or not, they have clumsy limbs.
PUCK. Don't tread so heavily, like elephant-calves! And let the clumsiest on this day be sturdy Puck himself.
ARIEL. If kindly nature gave you wings—if the spirit gave you wings—follow my light track up to the hill of roses!
ORCHESTRA (PIANISSIMO). Drifting clouds and wreathed mists brighten from on high! A breeze in the leaves, a wind in the rushes, and everything dissolves away.
[FAUST. MEPHISTOPHELES.]

FAUST. In misery! In despair! Long wandering the earth in piteous wretchedness, and now imprisoned! That sweet, hapless creature shut up in a dungeon, condemned to dreadful torments—and you have hidden it from me all this while! Stand here, stand there, then; roll your devil's eyes spitefully in your skull! Stand and defy me with your unbearable presence! Imprisoned! In hopeless misery! Given over to evil spirits and the merciless judgement of mankind! And meanwhile you lull me with insipid distractions, conceal her growing horror from me, and leave her to perish without help!
MEPHISTOPHELES. She is not the first.

FAUST. Dog! Loathsome monster! Change him back, you infinite Spirit, change this worm again into his dog-shape, in which he so often used to trot before me at night, to roll before the harmless wanderer's feet and hang from the shoulders of the man who fell. Change him back into his favourite shape, that he may crawl on his belly in the sand before me, that I may trample the reprobate underfoot!

chapters.title: A Gloomy Day. Open Country
paragraphs: [FAUST. MEPHISTOPHELES.]

FAUST. In misery! Despairing! Wandering the earth so long in piteous wretchedness, and now imprisoned! That sweet, hapless creature locked up in a dungeon, condemned as a criminal to dreadful torments! To that! To that! Treacherous, worthless spirit—and all this you have hidden from me! Stand here, just stand there. Roll your devil's eyes infuriated in your skull! Stand and defy me with your unbearable presence! A prisoner! In hopeless misery! Given over to evil spirits and the condemning, unfeeling judgement of mankind! And all the while, you have been lulling me with insipid distractions, hiding her growing wretchedness from me, and leaving her to perish without help.
MEPHISTOPHELES. She is not the first.

FAUST. Dog! Horrible monster! Change him back, you Infinite Spirit, change this creature into his dog's shape again, in which he so often used to trot before me at night, to roll before the harmless wanderer's feet and fasten onto the shoulders of the man who fell. Change him back into his favourite shape, that he may crawl before me on his belly in the sand, while I spurn him underfoot, the reprobate!

FAUST. Not the first! Woe! Woe! No human soul can grasp it—that more than one creature has sunk into so deep an abyss of misery; that the writhing death-agony of the first was not enough to atone for the guilt of all the rest in the eyes of the Ever-pardoning. The misery of this one harrows my marrow and my very life; and you stand grinning placidly at the fate of thousands.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Here we are at our wits' end again, just at the point where the senses of you mortals snap from over-straining. Why do you enter into fellowship with us, if you cannot see it through? You want to fly, and you are not safe from dizziness? Did we force ourselves on you, or you on us?

FAUST. Don't gnash your greedy teeth at me so defiantly! It disgusts me! Great, glorious Spirit, you who deigned to appear to me, you who know my heart and my soul, why yoke me to this shame-companion, who feeds on mischief and fattens on ruin?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Are you done?
FAUST. Save her, or woe to you! The most horrible curse upon you for thousands of years!
MEPHISTOPHELES. I cannot loosen the avenger's shackles, nor undo his bolts. Save her! Who was it that plunged her to ruin—I, or you?
[FAUST looks wildly around.]

MEPHISTOPHELES. Are you grasping after the thunder? Well, that it was not given to you wretched mortals! To dash an innocent reply to pieces—that is just the tyrant's way of venting himself in his perplexities.
FAUST. Take me to her! She shall be free!

MEPHISTOPHELES. And the danger you are exposing yourself to? Know this: the guilt of blood, shed by your hand, still lies upon the town. Avenging spirits hover above the place where he was slain, and lie in wait for the murderer's return.
FAUST. That too from you? Murder and death of a world upon you, monster! Take me to her, I say, and free her!

MEPHISTOPHELES. I will take you there—and what I can do, hear now. Do I have all power in heaven and on earth? I will cloud the jailer's senses; you possess yourself of the keys and carry her out with a human hand. I will keep watch! The magic horses will be ready, and I will spirit you away. This much I can do.
FAUST. Up and away!
[NIGHT. OPEN FIELD. FAUST and MEPHISTOPHELES, rushing along on black horses.]
FAUST. What are they weaving there around the Raven Stone?
MEPHISTOPHELES. I do not know what they are brewing and busying themselves with.
FAUST. They are soaring up, soaring down, bowing and bending.
MEPHISTOPHELES. A witch-guild.
FAUST. They are strewing and consecrating something.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Pass on! Pass on!
FAUST. Save her, save her!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Ride on! Ride on!
FAUST. Onward!

chapters.title: Night. Open Field
paragraphs: [FAUST and MEPHISTOPHELES rushing along upon black horses.]
FAUST. What are they weaving over there—those creatures around the Raven Stone?
MEPHISTOPHELES. I can't tell what they're cooking and contriving.
FAUST. They're waving upward, waving downward, bowing and stooping.
MEPHISTOPHELES. A witches' company.
FAUST. They are sprinkling and casting their charms.
MEPHISTOPHELES. On! On!
FAUST. The whole misery of mankind grips me. She lives here, behind this damp wall, and her crime was a fond delusion!
MEPHISTOPHELES. You hesitate to go in to her?
FAUST. Why do I tremble? Why do I shudder so?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Hurry on! Your delay costs her her life.
FAUST. I will not falter! Forward—I must save her!
MEPHISTOPHELES. The horses know the way. Onward, then, into the night!

chapters.title: Dungeon
paragraphs: [FAUST, with a bunch of keys and a lamp, before an iron wicket.] A trembling, long unfelt, seizes me; the concentrated misery of all mankind takes hold of me. Here, behind these damp walls, is where she lives, and her crime was a dear delusion! You hesitate to go to her! You fear to see her again! On! Your delay will be her death.
[He takes hold of the lock. Singing within.]
My mother, the harlot, who killed me! My father, the rogue, who ate me up! My little sister laid my bones in a cool place; and there I became a beautiful little wood-bird. Fly away! Fly away!
FAUST (OPENING THE LOCK). She does not suspect that her lover is listening, that he hears the chains clank, the straw rustle. [He enters.]
MARGARET (HIDING HER FACE IN THE BED OF STRAW). Woe! Woe! They are coming. Bitter death!
FAUST (SOFTLY). Hush! Hush! I have come to free you.
MARGARET (THROWING HERSELF BEFORE HIM). If you are human, feel for my wretchedness.
FAUST. You will wake the guard with your cries!
[He takes hold of the chains to unlock them.]

MARGARET (ON HER KNEES). Who gave you, headsman, this power over me? You come for me when it is still midnight. Be merciful and let me live. Isn't tomorrow morning soon enough? [She rises.] I am still so young, so young! And am I to die already? I was beautiful too, and that was my undoing! My true love stood close to me—now he is far away. My wreath lies torn, the flowers scattered. Don't take hold of me so roughly! Spare me! What have I done to you? Don't let me plead in vain! I have never seen you before in all my life, you know!
FAUST. Can I endure this misery?

MARGARET. I am entirely in your power now. Only let me first nurse my child. I held it to my heart the whole night through. They took it away to torture me, and now they say I killed it. I shall never be happy again. They sing songs about me! It's wicked of the people. An old tale ends so—who told them to apply it to me?
FAUST (THROWS HIMSELF ON THE GROUND). A lover lies at your feet, to loosen the bonds of your wretchedness.
MARGARET (THROWS HERSELF DOWN BESIDE HIM). Yes, let us kneel and call upon the saints. Look, under these steps, under the threshold, hell is seething! The Evil One, in fearful fury, is making a din.
FAUST (PASSIONATELY). Margaret! Margaret!

MARGARET (ALOUD). That was my true love's voice. [She springs up; the chains fall off.] Where is he? I heard him call. I am free! No one shall stop me. I will fly to his neck, lie on his breast! He called Margaret! He stood upon the threshold. Amid the howling and clattering of hell, amid the grim, devilish jeering, I recognized the sweet, the loving tone again.
FAUST. It is I.

MARGARET. It is you! Oh, say it once again! [Clasping him.] It is he! It is he! Where is all my wretchedness now? Where the agony of the dungeon, of the chains? It is you! You have come to save me. I am saved! And there already is the street, where I saw you for the first time, and the cheerful garden where Martha and I were waiting for you.
FAUST (STRIVING TO TAKE HER AWAY). Come! Come with me!
MARGARET. Oh, stay! I love to stay where you stay.
[Caressing him.]
FAUST. Hurry! If you don't hurry, we'll pay dearly for it.

MARGARET. What? You can no longer kiss? Such a little while away from me, my love, and you have already forgotten how to kiss! Why do I feel so anxious on your neck, when once a whole heaven came over me from your words, your looks, and you kissed me as if you would smother me? Kiss me! Or I will kiss you! [She embraces him.] Oh, woe! Your lips are cold—are dumb. Where have you left your love? Who has stolen it from me? [She turns from him.]
FAUST. Come! Follow me! Take courage, my love! I will press you to my heart with a thousandfold warmth—only follow me! I ask only this of you.
MARGARET (TURNING TO HIM). And is it really you, then? Is it truly you?
FAUST. It is I. Come along!
MARGARET. You are unlocking my chains, you are taking me to your arms again! How is it that you are not afraid of me? And do you know, my love, whom you are setting free?
FAUST. Come, come! The deep of the night is already passing.

MARGARET. I have killed my mother, I have drowned my child. Wasn't it given to you and me—to you, too? It is you! I can scarcely believe it. Give me your hand. It is no dream—your dear hand! But oh, it is damp! Wipe it off. I think there is blood on it. Oh, God! What have you done? Put up your sword! I beg you, do!
FAUST. Let what is past be past. You are killing me.

MARGARET. No, you must outlive me! I'll describe the graves to you; you must see to them first thing tomorrow. Give my mother the best place; my brother close beside her; me, a little to one side, only not too far off! And the little one on my right breast; no one else shall lie beside me. To nestle close to your side—that was a sweet, a dear delight! But I can do it no longer; I feel as if I have to force myself upon you, as if you were pushing me away. And yet it is you, and you look so kind, so good.
FAUST. If you feel that it is I, come along.
MARGARET. Out there?
FAUST. Into the open air!
MARGARET. If the grave is outside, if death lies in wait—then come! Out from here into the eternal resting-place, and not a step further. You are going away now? Oh Henry, if only I could go too!
FAUST. You can! You need only will it! The door stands open.

MARGARET. I dare not go out; there is no hope for me. What good is it to flee? They are lying in wait for me. It is so wretched to have to beg—and with an evil conscience too. So wretched to wander in a strange land—and they'll catch me, however I try.
FAUST. I will be with you.

MARGARET. Quick, quick! Save your poor child. Away! Take the path up by the brook—over the bridge—into the wood—to the left where the plank is—in the pond. Quick, grab hold of it! It is trying to rise! It is still struggling! Save it! Save it!
FAUST. Be calm, I beg you! Only one step, and you are free.

MARGARET. If only we were past the hill! There sits my mother on a stone—my brain grows cold!—there sits my mother on a stone, and shakes her head. She does not beckon, she does not nod, her head is heavy; she slept so long, she will wake no more. She slept so that we might enjoy ourselves. Those were happy times!
FAUST. Since no prayer, no persuasion is of any use here, I will take the risk of carrying you out.
MARGARET. Let me go! No, I will not endure violence! Don't lay hold of me so murderously! You know I have done everything else to please you.
FAUST. The day is dawning! My love! My love!

MARGARET. Day! Yes, day is coming on! The last day is breaking! It was to have been my wedding day! Tell no one you had been with Margaret already. Woe to my wreath! It is all over now! We shall meet again—but not at the dance. The crowd is thickening; it cannot be heard. The square, the streets, cannot contain them. The bell tolls! The wand is broken! How they bind me and seize me! Already I am dragged off to the place of blood! Already, for every neck, the sharp steel quivers that quivers for mine. The world lies dumb as the grave!
FAUST. Oh, that I had never been born!
MEPHISTOPHELES (APPEARS OUTSIDE). Up! Or you are lost. Vain hesitation! Lingering and prattling! My horses are shivering; the morning is breaking through.
MARGARET. What is rising up out of the floor? He! He! Send him away! What does he want at this holy place? He has come for me! FAUST. You shall live!
MARGARET. Judgement of God! I have given myself up to you.
MEPHISTOPHELES (TO FAUST). Come! Come! I will leave you in the lurch with her.
MARGARET. Yours am I, Father! Save me! You angels! You holy hosts, gather around me to protect me! Henry! I shudder to look at you.
MEPHISTOPHELES. She is judged! VOICE FROM ABOVE. Is saved.
MEPHISTOPHELES (TO FAUST). To me, this way!
[He disappears with FAUST.]
VOICE (FROM WITHIN, DYING AWAY). Henry! Henry!
